newsitem.title: USA: K.C. Fed's Hoenig says US economy growing solidly.
newsitem.headline: K.C. Fed's Hoenig says US economy growing solidly.

text.p: The U.S. economy continues to grow at a solid pace with tight labor markets, strong consumer demand and moderate inflation, but price pressure risks are "on the upside," said Thomas Hoenig, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.
"Virtually all sectors of the economy are growing solidly," Hoenig told an audience here during a joint board meeting of the Kansas City Fed.
The swift pace of economic expansion in the fourth quarter of last year appears to have "carried over" into early 1997, Hoenig said.

"Is the growth in demand we've seen over the last six months sustainable over the next year and a half without some increase of inflation? To be sure, the evidence is mixed, but there are signs that inflation risks are on the upside," he added.

Signs of inflation pressure appear in the U.S. unemployment rate, which read 5.2 percent in March, and the capacity utilization rate within the manufacturing sector, reported at 83.3 percent last month, Hoenig said.
Describing the dangers of high levels of resource utilization, Hoenig said "aggregate demand may be growing faster than aggregate supply."
Factors that contributed to favorable inflation trends in 1996 may be of "unknown duration," he said.
In particular, job insecurity and decelerating benefits cost inflation helped restrain growth in overall labor compensation, he explained.
Both factors, Hoenig said, could evaporate.
"Anecdotal reports here in the 10th (Fed) district and elsewhere suggest labor markets are tightening," he said.
But the regional bank president mentioned some "encouraging signs" to keep in mind.
He noted "the appreciation of the dollar we have seen should help restrain inflation" and added that the Fed has an "obligation" to preserve the value of the dollar.
Hoenig asserted there is no tradeoff between growth and inflation that would suggest the Fed should tolerate a "little more inflation" to achieve a "little more growth."
And he reasserted that the central bank needs to act against inflation expectations.

"Even moderate inflation leads to inflation uncertainty, real growth variability and relative price volatility," Hoenig said. "Low levels of inflation and inflation expectations have been a key support for healthy economic performance."
Looking ahead, Hoenig projected economic growth between 2.0 and 3.0 percent for 1997, adding that the economic environment "requires vigilance."
